title: Shreyas Iyer Backs Vaibhav Sooryavanshi: 'When His Time Comes, He'll Dominate Indian Cricket'
excerpt: India's T20I captain praised the 15-year-old's quiet dressing-room presence and destructive batting, predicting Vaibhav Sooryavanshi will dominate Indian cricket once his opportunity arrives.
body:
• Speaking on JioHotstar's 'Follow the Blues: Sarpanch Shreyas' ahead of the West Indies T20I series, Shreyas Iyer said Vaibhav Sooryavanshi “is going to dominate Indian cricket” when his time comes.
  • The 15-year-old stays in India's 15 as backup while Sanju Samson and Abhishek Sharma open; he scored 53 runs at a strike rate of 176.66 in two Asian Games outings.
  • Sooryavanshi became the youngest Indian to win an Asian Games gold medal — 15 years and 190 days — in India's 19-run win over Pakistan on October 3; his 19-ball fifty in Zimbabwe made him the youngest player in international cricket history to register a half-century.
  • The five-match West Indies T20I series begins October 6 at 7:00 PM IST in Lucknow, live on JioHotstar and Star Sports.

Shreyas Iyer has seen 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi up close, and he likes what he sees. Speaking on JioHotstar's 'Follow the Blues: Sarpanch Shreyas' ahead of India's five-match T20I series against the West Indies, the India captain backed the teenage opener to become a dominant force — just not quite yet.

“And I know that his time will come, because we have been playing with World Cup-winning openers right now... when his time comes, he is going to dominate Indian cricket.”

— Shreyas Iyer, India T20I captain

The context is the bench hierarchy ahead of the West Indies series, which opens October 6. With Samson and Abhishek operating as the first-choice opening pair, Sooryavanshi is expected to serve as a backup rather than a starter. Iyer said the established openers have earned their time through proven track records — while the teenager stays in the squad of 15, learning the demands of international cricket without the weight of immediate expectation.

The quiet kid and the destructive batter

What fascinates Iyer about Sooryavanshi is the contrast. Off the field, the teenager barely speaks; on it, he dismantles attacks. Iyer described deliberately steering their conversations away from cricket — everyone talks to the boy about cricket — and toward his family, his lifestyle, what he does beyond the game, because that is when Sooryavanshi opens up and becomes himself.

“He's a very charming, sweet guy to interact with and good to have him around the dressing room,” Iyer said. “And a very silent guy, but on the field, is very destructive. So, that's like an irony when you look at him.”

That destruction showed at the Asian Games in Japan, where India took gold. Sooryavanshi struck 38 off 21 against Sri Lanka in the semi-final, then 15 off nine balls in the final against Pakistan — including two sixes — before Saim Ayub dismissed him. Ayub mocked the teenager with a ‘baby’ rocking celebration; Abhishek answered with a six and two fours off the rest of the over. India won by 19 runs, and at 15 years and 190 days Sooryavanshi became the youngest Indian ever to win Asian Games gold, breaking shooter Saurabh Chaudhary's record from 2018.

The numbers behind the patience

The numbers explain both the hype and the wait. After a July 2026 debut against England, Sooryavanshi has 243 runs in eight T20Is at an average of 30.75 — including a 19-ball fifty that made him the youngest player in international cricket history to register a half-century. His Asian Games return: 53 runs in two innings at a strike rate of 176.66.

The incumbents are formidable: Abhishek has 62 T20Is at a career strike rate near 195 and offers left-arm spin as a tactical bonus; Samson brings 72 T20Is, elite wicketkeeping and multiple international centuries. Iyer's rule is winning before experimenting — early lineup changes, he said, make players insecure.

A dressing room that has his back

Abhishek Sharma, whose opening slot Sooryavanshi is waiting on, has been equally vocal: the seniors, he said, feel a responsibility to make the teenager comfortable.

“He is a very smart guy... we all know what he has achieved and that he belongs here. All of us, his elder brothers, are here for him.”

— Abhishek Sharma, India opener

For the diaspora, the Sooryavanshi story is irresistible: a 15-year-old rewriting record books in India blue, handled with unusual care by his captain. The West Indies series — Lucknow on October 6, then Ranchi, Indore, Hyderabad and Bengaluru — will be watched as much for whether the teenager gets a game as for the results.

What's next

Perspective matters: when the 2028 T20 World Cup arrives, Sooryavanshi will still be 17. Being on the bench at 15 is a structured development path, not a snub, and his early numbers say he belongs at this level. Whether form forces the issue in the West Indies series or not, Iyer's prediction now hangs over the teenager's career: his time will come, and then, the captain says, he will dominate.
